```{r}
#| label: libraries
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# The first thing I would explore is the distribution and types of variables. I can begin by simply looking at the data with head() or glimpse(). 
```{r}
#| label: looking at the data
final_data <- read_csv(
  here("data", "processed", "final_data.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
head(final_data)
glimpse(final_data)
```

# Then I would generate summary statistics for numeric variables (such as maternal mortality  ratio, newborn mortality, etc.) using the summary() function. 
```{r}
#| label: summary stats
final_data |> 
    summary()
```

# To get a better understanding of the limits of these summary statistics, I could randomly remove values of the statistic for certain countries and then see how the summary statistics change depending on the group of countries with missing data. 
```{r}
#| label: limits of. summary stats
sample_means <- tibble(seed = c(), mean = c(), states_ignored = c())

for (i in c(1:5)) {
  set.seed(i)
  dont_get <- c(sample(x = state.name, size = 5))
  sample_means <-
    sample_means |>
    rbind(tibble(
      seed = i,
      mean =
        us_populations |>
          filter(!state %in% dont_get) |>
          summarise(mean = mean(population)) |>
          pull(),
      states_ignored = str_c(dont_get, collapse = ", ")
    ))
}

sample_means |>
  tt() |> 
  style_tt(j = 1:3, align = "lrr") |> 
  format_tt(digits = 0, num_mark_big = ",", num_fmt = "decimal") |> 
  setNames(c("Seed", "Mean", "Ignored states"))
```

# I could also use graphs to map the distribution of variables with a logarithmic transformation of the y-values where appropriate. 

# This may help identify outliers, which I could explore further for patterns with other variables.

# I could look at the variable types using the table() function and see where expected variable types do not match. Once I am done observing the kinds and distributions of the variables, I would explore the degree, extent, and kinds of missingness, as the preliminary glimpse into the data would reveal that there is quite a bit of missingness in the armed conflict data.
